content: Subdural empyema is a collection of purulent material located between the dura mater and the arachnoid membrane, typically resulting from an infection. The causative pathogens responsible for subdural empyema vary, with some being more common than others. The most frequently encountered pathogen is Streptococcus milleri. Other common pathogens include various species of streptococci and enterococci, as well as aerobic Gram-negative bacilli such as Haemophilus influenzae, Proteus, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, Salmonella, Morganella, and Eikenella. In some cases, no microbial growth is observed despite clinical evidence of infection. Less commonly, subdural empyema may be caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, or coagulase-negative staphylococci. Anaerobic organisms can also be implicated, including anaerobic Gram-positive cocci such as Veillonella and Peptostreptococcus, as well as anaerobic Gram-negative bacilli like Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, and Prevotella. Empiric antimicrobial therapy is initiated when the source of infection is unclear. For intracranial subdural empyema of unknown origin, the preferred regimen includes a combination of (Nafcillin 2 g IV every 4 hours or Oxacillin 2 g IV every 4 hours) AND (Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours or Cefotaxime 8–12 g/day IV every 4–6 hours) AND Metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg IV every 6 hours. When intracranial subdural empyema is associated with sinusitis or otitis media, the same regimen is recommended: (Nafcillin 2 g IV every 4 hours or Oxacillin 2 g IV every 4 hours) AND (Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours or Cefotaxime 8–12 g/day IV every 4–6 hours) AND Metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg IV every 6 hours. For cases of intracranial subdural empyema following cranial trauma, the preferred treatment is either Nafcillin 2 g IV every 4 hours or Oxacillin 2 g IV every 4 hours. In patients with intracranial subdural empyema following neurosurgical procedures, the recommended regimen includes Vancomycin 30–45 mg/kg/day IV every 8–12 hours AND Ceftazidime 2 g IV every 8 hours. In neonates, subdural empyema is often associated with meningitis. For infants younger than 1 month, the preferred regimen is Ampicillin 200 mg/kg/day IV every 4 hours AND Cefotaxime 200 mg/kg/day IV every 6 hours. For infants aged 1–3 months, the regimen includes Ampicillin 200 mg/kg/day IV every 4 hours AND either Cefotaxime 200 mg/kg/day IV every 6 hours OR Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day IV every 12 hours. For infants older than 3 months, the recommended treatment is Vancomycin 60 mg/kg/day IV every 6 hours AND one of the following: Cefotaxime 200 mg/kg/day IV every 6 hours, Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day IV every 12 hours, or Cefepime 150 mg/kg/day IV every 8 hours. For spinal subdural empyema, the preferred treatment is either Nafcillin 2 g IV every 4 hours or Oxacillin 2 g IV every 4 hours. Pathogen-directed antimicrobial therapy is tailored based on the specific organism identified. For methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), the preferred regimen is Vancomycin 30–45 mg/kg/day IV every 8–12 hours for 4–6 weeks. Alternative options include Linezolid 600 mg orally or IV every 12 hours for 4–6 weeks, or Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) 5 mg/kg/dose orally or IV every 8–12 hours for 4–6 weeks. In pediatric patients, the recommended dose of Vancomycin is 15 mg/kg/dose IV every 6 hours, or Linezolid 10 mg/kg/dose orally or IV every 8 hours.
